old: *Ir a + infinitivo* expresses an intention or a plan connected to the present. It is useful when preparation or a decision already exists.
new: You know *ir a* + infinitive from A1. In B1 you use it for plans you have already made, usually with a reason. This lesson adds three expressions that are new: *planear* and *tener previsto* (to plan) and *estar a punto de* (to be about to).
why: B1 screen presents A1 ir a as new: recap

old: We're going to leave early so that we don't have to wait.
new: We're going to leave early because we want to arrive before eight.
why: english of the replaced example

old: Marta is going to study in Chile next year.
new: Marta plans to study in Chile next year.
why: english

old: If you could already say *\"I've decided...\"* before opening your mouth, reach for *ir a* + infinitive — it presents a plan that exists in the speaker's mind before the moment of speaking, not a fresh guess about the future.
new: Reach for *ir a* + infinitive when the plan already exists before you speak, often with a reason: *Voy a estudiar más porque quiero aprender*. *Estar a punto de* + infinitive is for something that starts in a moment.
why: tip tidied (no 'fresh guess' claim; mentions the new expression)

old: The simple future expresses predictions, expectations and future results. It is common when the speaker presents an event as expected rather than already arranged.
new: You know the simple future from A2 Unit 19. Use it for predictions, expectations and future results: the speaker presents an event as expected rather than already arranged. Here you use it with *creo que* to make predictions.
why: recap: simple future is A2 Unit 19

old: A common slip: after *si* in a realistic condition, the *si*-clause itself stays in the present, never the future — *si sales ahora*, not *si saldrás ahora*. The future belongs in the other clause, where the result lands.
new: Future endings are added to the whole infinitive: *terminar* becomes *terminaremos*, *encontrar* becomes *encontraremos*. A few verbs change the stem, for example *tener* becomes *tendrá* and *haber* becomes *habrá*.
why: tip taught si-clauses (b1-08-04) before its screen; replaced with a point about the future itself

old: Expressions of wishes, hopes and desires can introduce the present subjunctive. With *esperar que* and similar structures, the second clause normally has a different subject.
new: You know the present subjunctive after wishes and hopes from A2 Unit 27. With *esperar que*, *querer que*, *desear que* and *ojalá*, the verb of the second clause is in the subjunctive and normally has a different subject. This lesson adds the words *deseo*, *conseguir* and *alcanzar*.
why: recap: A2 Unit 27

old: I want you to arrive early so we can talk beforehand.
new: I want you to arrive early because we have an appointment.
why: english

old: I hope we find a solution that works for everyone.
new: I hope we find a solution for everyone.
why: english

old: *Ir a + infinitivo* normally presents an existing intention. The simple future is often more suitable for predictions, expectations or future results.
new: You know both forms: *ir a* + infinitive from A1 and the simple future from A2 Unit 19. *Ir a* normally presents an existing intention. The simple future is often more suitable for predictions, expectations or future results. In everyday speech the two often overlap.
why: recap

old: English \"will\" and \"going to\" blur together in casual speech, but Spanish keeps the line sharper: a hotel you've already booked is *voy a reservarlo*, while a guess about its price next August is *será caro*.
new: A safe guide: use *voy a* + infinitive for something you have already decided (*voy a reservar el hotel*) and the future for a guess (*creo que será más caro*).
why: tip overstated that Spanish keeps the two sharply apart

old: Natural future talk combines plans, predictions, wishes and conditions. A connected account may move between *ir a + infinitivo*, the simple future and the subjunctive.
new: You know all of these forms: *ir a* + infinitive (A1), the simple future (A2 Unit 19) and the present subjunctive after hopes (A2 Unit 27). A connected account moves between them: plans, predictions, wishes and conditions.
why: recap

old: I hope the trip is calm, although there will surely be some delay.
new: I hope the trip is calm, although I think there will be some problem.
why: english

old: If everything goes well, we'll reach the goal before the month ends.
new: If everything goes well, we'll reach the goal within a month.
why: english

new: Notice how these four sentences use four different forms, each answering a different question: *voy a salir* (a plan), *espero que sea* (a wish), *alcanzaremos* (a prediction that depends on a condition) and *estamos a punto de* (something about to happen).
